title: TICOVAC (tick-borne encephalitis vaccine) injection [Pfizer Laboratories Div Pfizer Inc]
content: The National Library of Medicine report on the TICOVAC tick‑borne encephalitis vaccine summarizes safety data from ten clinical trials involving 3,240 children (ages 1–15) and 4,427 adults (ages 16 and older). In Study 209, a multicenter, open‑label trial, 2,417 children received three doses (Day 0, 1, and 6 months). Local and systemic solicited adverse reactions were recorded for four days after each dose; fever incidence by age group is detailed in Table 3. Less than 1 % of children reported additional reactions such as vertigo, dizziness, sensory abnormalities, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dyspepsia, injection‑site pruritus, and urticaria. Study 208, a randomized, single‑blind comparison, enrolled 3,966 adults who received two vaccinations with either TICOVAC or a non‑US licensed TBE vaccine; Study 213 followed up with a third TICOVAC dose (N = 3,705). Solicited local and systemic reactions for doses 1–3 are presented in Table 4, with additional reactions (<1 %) including hypersensitivity, somnolence, vertigo, diarrhea, abdominal pain, injection‑site pruritus, and warmth. Follow‑up studies (700401 and 223) assessed antibody persistence and booster response; 156 subjects received a 0.25 mL fourth dose and 240 received a 0.5 mL dose. Table 5 shows solicited reactions after the booster. Serious adverse events (SAEs) and deaths were reported in 62 children (1 death) and 54 adults (2 deaths), none deemed related to the vaccine; only one child’s febrile convulsion was possibly related (Study 197). The data indicate that TICOVAC’s safety profile is consistent with expectations for a TBE vaccine, with no serious events linked to the product.

title: Valneva:  Positive Phase 2 data in Lyme disease
content: Valneva announced that its Phase 2 study of the Lyme disease vaccine candidate VLA15 has produced positive immunogenicity and safety results. The data show a strong immune response in both children and adults after the third annual booster, and a robust anamnestic response for all six serotypes. An independent data monitoring committee reported no safety concerns in any age group, mirroring earlier booster outcomes and supporting the potential benefit of a booster before each Lyme disease season. VLA15 is the most advanced Lyme vaccine candidate, with two Phase 3 trials underway; Phase 3 vaccinations have been completed and, if the data remain positive, Pfizer plans to submit marketing‑authorization applications in the US and EU in 2026. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that approximately 476,000 people are diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease each year in the United States, and 132,000 cases are reported annually in Europe.

title: Lassa fever vaccine expected by 2032 - MyJoyOnline
content: A Lassa fever vaccine could be available by 2032, according to health experts in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. Phase 1 trials are finished and Phase 2a is underway; the total projected cost is between $225 million and $340 million, with $185 million earmarked for clinical development, $25 million for chemistry, manufacturing and controls, and $13 million for commercial readiness at Institut Pasteur de Dakar (IPD). Phase 2b is slated to start in 2026, requiring up to $28 million for clinical development and $15 million for a bridging study, while a technology transfer to a new contract development and manufacturing organisation (CDMO) will need up to $3 million. Manufacturing scale‑up for Phase 3 is planned for 2027 at a cost of up to $8 million, and Phase 3 itself will begin in 2028 with estimated costs of $150 million to $250 million. Additional medium‑term expenses include up to $13.6 million for GMP Phase 3 clinical trial material and $8.9 million for late‑stage supporting activities. The vaccine candidate is being tested in Ghana, Liberia and Nigeria; the IAVI C105 trial involves 612 participants, including adults, adolescents and children aged two years and older, and will monitor safety and immune response for six months, with some followed for two years. CEPI and Wellcome have already provided $6.4 million to the University of Texas Medical Branch for the UNVEIL project, which seeks immune markers that could replace lengthy efficacy trials. "The Phase 1 trial started in 2018, and by 2025, we will be halfway through production. In just a few more years, we will have a vaccine for Lassa fever," Dr. Henshaw Amandi told JoyNews. "Once we can measure protection in a blood test instead of a prolonged clinical efficacy trial, we can deliver vaccines to impacted communities much faster," Dr. Courtney B. Woolsey added. Dr. Katrin Ramsauer noted that identifying immune markers would be a milestone and could help tackle other hemorrhagic‑fever pathogens. Lassa fever, first described in 1969, remains a priority disease for the World Health Organization; it affects up to 300,000 people annually in West Africa, with a 20 % fatality rate among hospitalized patients, and survivors often suffer permanent hearing loss or miscarriage in pregnancy.

title: Elucidated protein structures in the malaria parasite offer opportunities for new vaccines
content: Researchers from Radboud University Medical Center and The Hospital for Sick Children Research Institute in Toronto have successfully elucidated the 3D structures of two key proteins in the malaria parasite using cryo-electron microscopy, analyzing millions of microscope images magnified up to 130,000 times. This breakthrough, published in the journal Immunity (2025), was made possible after culturing 30 billion malaria parasites over six months to extract sufficient protein material. The proteins, known since the 1980s but previously structurally unknown due to their difficulty in production, are part of a complex involved in the parasite’s sexual reproduction and are specific to the malaria pathogen, making them ideal vaccine targets. According to Ph.D. candidate Ezra Bekkering and researcher Matthijs Jore, understanding the proteins’ atomic-level structure enables scientists to design new transmission-blocking vaccines that prevent the parasite from developing in mosquitoes. While existing malaria vaccines offer partial protection and do not stop transmission, these new vaccines aim to interrupt the spread from person to mosquito. The study provides a structural blueprint for future vaccine development, with the potential to contribute significantly to global malaria eradication efforts. The findings are detailed in the paper 'Cryo-EM structure of endogenous Pfs230:Pfs48/45 complex with six antibodies reveals mechanisms of malaria transmission-blocking activity,' DOI: 10.1016/j.immuni.2025.09.014.

title: Impfung verhinderte 10.000 Erkrankungen
content: A study by experts from the Medical University of Vienna, published in the journal 'Vaccine', analyzed lab-confirmed cases of tick-borne encephalitis (FSME) in Austria from 2000 to 2024. The findings indicate that the FSME vaccination prevented more than 10,000 hospitalizations, over 4,000 severe cases, and 80 deaths during this period. The study evaluated 2,260 hospitalizations due to FSME, with adults aged 16–59 most affected, followed by those over 60; 12% of cases involved children under 15. Among hospitalized patients, 1,000 experienced severe disease courses, and 26 (1.2%) died. No causal treatment exists for FSME, which can lead to serious neurological long-term effects. The study confirms that consistent vaccination offers approximately 99% protection, while irregular but ongoing booster doses provide over 90% protection. Despite high vaccination rates in Austria—among the highest in Europe—the proportion of people receiving recommended vaccinations has declined over time. This trend coincides with a significant rise in FSME cases among under- or non-vaccinated individuals. The researchers emphasize that sustained high vaccination coverage is essential to prevent further increases in cases and to significantly reduce the burden on Austria’s healthcare system.

title: VALNEVA (EPA:VLA) | Valneva annonce de nouvelles données positives d'innocuité et d'immunogénicité de Phase 2 pour le candidat vaccin contre la maladie de Lyme
content:
Valneva SE announced on 3 September 2025 that its Phase 2 study (VLA15‑221) of the Lyme disease vaccine candidate VLA15 has produced positive immunogenicity and safety results. After a third annual booster dose, participants aged 5–11 years, 12–17 years and 18–65 years showed a strong immune response, with 100 % seroconversion for all six OspA serotypes (confidence interval 96.7 %–100 %). The geometric mean antibody titres one month after the first and second booster doses were similarly high. The independent Data Monitoring Committee reported no safety concerns in any age group or treatment arm. The data support the potential benefit of a yearly booster before each Lyme season.

Valneva highlighted that no human Lyme vaccine currently exists; VLA15 is the most advanced candidate, with two Phase 3 trials underway (VALOR and C4601012). The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate that about 476 000 people are diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease annually in the United States, and 132 000 cases are reported each year in Europe. The Phase 2 trial enrolled 560 healthy participants (190 on a 0‑2‑6 month schedule, 181 on a 0‑6 month schedule, 189 receiving placebo). Pfizer and Valneva entered a collaboration in April 2020 to develop and commercialise VLA15.

Juan Carlos Jaramillo, MD, Valneva’s medical director, said, 'Ces nouvelles données confirment davantage le bénéfice potentiel des doses de rappel dans toutes les tranches d'âge évaluées.' The press release also notes that the vaccine targets the OspA protein on the surface of Borrelia burgdorferi, blocking transmission from ticks to humans.

The announcement is part of Valneva’s broader portfolio, which includes vaccines for travel, Shigellosis and Zika, and is supported by ongoing Phase 3 studies in endemic regions of North America and Europe.

title: Togo- Introduction du vaccin antipaludique R21 dès le 1er septembre 2025 -
content: The Togolese Ministry of Health and Public Hygiene is preparing to introduce the malaria vaccine R21 into the national immunisation schedule on 1 September 2025. A briefing held on 26 August 2025 in Lomé gathered parents, community leaders, journalists and education stakeholders to discuss the new schedule, coverage strategies and media mobilisation. Dr. Éric Gnassounou‑Akpa, head of the immunisation monitoring section, emphasised the vaccine’s safety and effectiveness, stating, 'Pour protéger les enfants, le gouvernement a décidé d’introduire le vaccin contre le paludisme à partir du 1er septembre 2025 dans notre pays. Ce sont les enfants de 5 mois qui vont bénéficier du vaccin dans nos formations sanitaires.' He added that a full course requires four doses at 5, 6, 7 and 15 months, and that the vaccine complements other tools such as insecticide‑treated nets, chemoprevention and intermittent preventive treatment for pregnant women. Participants pledged to disseminate information to achieve an 80 % coverage target for children aged five months and older. In Greater Lomé, malaria prevalence among children aged 6–59 months was 35.5 % in 2020, underscoring the need for additional interventions against Plasmodium falciparum.

title: We Have a Lyme Disease Vaccine. Why Don't We Use It?
content: The article explains Lyme disease, caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi carried by black‑legged ticks, and outlines its symptoms—flu‑like fever, chills, muscle and joint pain, and potentially severe complications such as Bell's palsy, meningitis, numb limbs, and heart problems. It describes the bacterium’s life cycle, noting that B. burgdorferi resides in the gut of immature ticks, spreads to the salivary glands, and is transmitted to mammals when the tick bites. The piece then recounts the history of the Lyme disease vaccine, noting that it was introduced in 1998 but has since been withdrawn from the human market, a fact the author frames as a cautionary tale for today’s antivax discourse. The article opens with the line, 'The tragic tale of LYMErix -- a chilling prequel to today's antivax movement,' and stresses that while the vaccine is no longer available to humans, it is still used in other contexts.

title: USA Vaccine Market Outlook Report 2025-2030 | Focus on Lassa Fever, Ebola, RSV Vaccines, Alongside Genomics-Driven Targeted Therapies, Strengthens Public Health Preparedness and Investment Potential
content:
The USA vaccine market is valued at about USD 30 billion, driven by public‑health initiatives, rising disease awareness, and advances in vaccine technology. Key players—Pfizer, Moderna, and Johnson & Johnson—dominate the market thanks to strong R&D, distribution networks, and brand recognition. The U.S. government supports vaccination through programs such as Vaccines for Children (VFC), which provides free vaccines to eligible children and aims to increase coverage among underserved populations. 

Growth drivers include a significant rise in infectious‑disease cases, with the CDC reporting over 2.8 million cases annually and an estimated $130 billion economic burden. Technological breakthroughs, especially mRNA and vector‑based platforms, led to a 30 % increase in R&D investment in 2023, totaling roughly $16 billion. Government funding has also surged, with billions allocated in 2024 to support immunization initiatives. 

Challenges remain: vaccine hesitancy fueled by misinformation lowers uptake, and supply‑chain disruptions have caused delays and shortages, raising operational costs. 

Future outlook points to substantial growth, particularly in mRNA and combination vaccines, personalized medicine, and targeted vaccines for emerging diseases such as Lassa fever, Ebola, and RSV. The market is expected to expand as public‑private partnerships improve distribution and accessibility. 

As quoted in the report, the 'USA Vaccine Market outlook to 2030' highlights that "the market is poised for substantial growth, driven by ongoing technological advancements and increased government support."

title: نجاح أول تجربة بشرية للقاح جديد ضد التيفود والسالمونيلا معا - اليوم السابع
content: Researchers at the Center for Vaccine Development at the University of Maryland School of Medicine successfully completed Phase 1 of clinical trials for a new experimental vaccine, the Trivalent Salmonella Conjugate Vaccine (TSCV), designed to protect against typhoid fever (typhoid) and non-typhoidal Salmonella, two leading causes of illness and death among children in sub-Saharan Africa. In a randomized, placebo-controlled trial, 22 healthy adults in the United States received either a low dose (6.25 micrograms) or high dose (12.5 micrograms) of TSCV, or a placebo. The vaccine was found to be safe and well-tolerated, with only mild, short-term pain at the injection site reported. All recipients of the vaccine showed strong immune responses to all three polysaccharide components, while none of the placebo recipients did. The vaccine elicited robust, balanced, and long-lasting antibody responses, even at the low dose, and activated a specific immune defense involving white blood cells that help eliminate infection—a response not previously observed with similar protein components. Some participants showed pre-existing antibodies, suggesting prior exposure through foodborne illness, which may have contributed to stronger and longer-lasting immunity. The study’s lead researcher, Wilbur Chen, stated the results are highly encouraging, indicating the vaccine could protect children in high-risk regions. In 2017, sub-Saharan Africa reported over 420,000 Salmonella cases and 66,000 deaths—mostly in children—while typhoid caused an additional 650,000 infections and nearly 9,000 deaths. A single vaccine offering protection against both diseases could represent a major leap in global child health.
